overview.body:
**Theía** ​(*theia*) — ‌The Sight ‌that ​Sees the ​Light ​— belongs ​to the ​Greek ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Titaness of ​Sight". The ‌name ​means "Goddess, ​divine"[^1].

Theía ​is ​the **Titaness ​of ‌sight, shining, ​and the ‌bright ​ether**. Though ‌less famous ​than ‌her children ​Hēlios, ‌Selḗnē, and ​Ēōs, she ​is ‌the luminous ‌source from ‌which ​they spring ​— ‌the divine ​principle that ​makes ‌seeing and ​being seen ​possible. ‌Hesiod gives ​her ‌one marriage ​and three ​children; ​Pindar gives ​her a ‌golden ‌hymn; the ​rest ‌is inference.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the ‌name as ‌**Theía** and ‌serves ‌its temple ​at ‌[theía.com](https://xn--thea-xpa.com). The ​restoration preserves ​stress ​— a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ​*theia* survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by ‌the early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Θεία**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Goddess, divine"[^1].

‌The ​ASCII form ​*theia* ‌survives only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system ​could not ​carry ​diacritics; it ​is ​a technological ‌compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration ‌**Theía** recovers ​the ‌stress accent ​of ​the original ‌directly ‌in the ‌address ​bar. The ​restoration ‌preserves ​stress — ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**t** ​→ ​**T** — ‌T ‌uppercase
- **h** ​→ ‌**h** — ​h ​same
- **e** ‌→ ‌**e** — ‌e ‌same
- ​**i** → ‌**í** ​— Acute ​on ​í — ‌in ​Θεία the ​accent ​falls on ‌the ​second ​element of ​the ‌diphthong ει
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ‌a same

​The ‌project holds ‌the ​domain ​**theía.com** (xn--thea-xpa.com) ​as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/tʰeː.ía/** ​— Attic ​Greek ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ‌**Th-** ​— Aspirated ​theta [tʰ], ‌the breathy ​initial ‌consonant.
- **-ē-** ​— Long ‌eta ​[ɛː], the ​first syllable's ​length.
- ​**-ía** — ​Short iota ‌with ​acute plus ‌alpha — ​the ‌pitch peak ​on the ‌second ​syllable.

For ‌the modern ​speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ‌'thay-EE-ah' — ‌the ​first syllable ​is long ‌and ​level, the ​second pitched ‌high ​and bright.

​Kindred and ‌historical ​forms of ‌the name:

- ​**Greek** ​— Θεία ​(Theía), Titaness ​of ‌sight, shining, ‌and the ​bright ‌upper air
- ​**Root** — ​θέα (théa), ‌'sight, ‌view'; related ‌to θεάομαι, ‌'to ​gaze'
- **Children** ‌— Hēlios, ​Selēnē, ​and Eōs ​— sun, ‌moon, ​and dawn

​Theía preserves ​both ‌features because ​the Greek ​Θεία ​contains both ‌length (η ​in ‌the first ​syllable) and ‌stress (acute ​on ‌the ι ‌of the ​second). ​She is ​the Titaness ​whose ‌children are ‌the celestial ​lights.

domains.body:
Theía ​is the ‌**Titaness of ‌sight, ​shining, and ​the ​bright ether**. ​Though less ​famous ‌than her ​children Hēlios, ​Selḗnē, ‌and Ēōs, ​she ‌is the ​luminous source ‌from ​which they ​spring — ​the ​divine principle ​that ‌makes seeing ​and being ‌seen ​possible. Hesiod ‌gives her ​one ‌marriage and ​three ‌children; Pindar ​gives her ​a ‌golden hymn; ‌the rest ‌is ​inference.[^1]

### Mother ​of ‌Lights

By ​Hyperion she ​bore ‌the sun, ​moon, and ​dawn ‌— every ​light ‌that crosses ​the sky ​(Theogony ​371–374).

### Goddess ​of Sight

‌Her ‌name belongs ​to ‌the root ​θέα, 'sight'; ​she ‌is the ‌shining by ‌which ‌anything is ​seen ‌at all.

### ​Shining Ether

​She ​personifies the ‌bright upper ​air ​through which ​light ‌travels to ​the eye ​— ​the medium, ‌not the ​lamp.

### ‌Titanic Lineage

​Daughter ‌of Ouranos ​and Gaia, ‌sister ‌of Kronos ​and Rhea, ​aunt ​of Zeus ​— ‌born with ‌the first ​generation.

sources.citation: Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Theía ​concentrates in ​a ​small set ​of ​recurring ‌attributes, each ​a ​compressed ‌statement about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- **The ​gold ‌crown** ​— Her ​Hesiodic ​attribute — ​'Theía, ​crowned ‌with gold' ​(Theogony ‌135) ​— radiance ‌worn ​as royalty.
- ‌**Radiant ​eyes** ‌— The ​organs ​of sight, ‌her ‌namesake ‌province; she ​is ​the ‌light by ​which ​seeing happens.
- ‌**Sun, ​moon, ​and dawn** ‌— ​Her three ‌children ​— ​the visible ​proof ​of her ‌marriage ‌to ​Hyperion, and ‌her ​true ​portrait.
- **The ‌bright ‌ether** — ‌The ‌luminous ​upper air ‌she ​personifies, through ​which ​every ‌ray descends ​to ​the ​world.
- **Flash ‌on ​gold and ​water** ​— ‌Pindar's image ​(Isthmian ‌5): her ​radiance ‌glimpsed ​on metal ‌and ‌on ​the sea ​— ​the sun's ​distant ‌gleam ‌that sailors ​read.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

mythology.body:
Theía has **no independent ​narrative myths**; her importance is genealogical and cosmological. ‌Through her, the Titans bequeath light to ‌the Olympian cosmos — and the tradition ​is honest enough to leave her otherwise silent. ​Two lines of Hesiod, an ode of ​Pindar, and a name that became a ​science are her whole surviving estate.[^1]

### Birth of ​the Luminaries (Genealogy)

Hesiod mentions Theía exactly ‌where her meaning lives. First, in the ​Titan catalogue, she is simply '**Theía, crowned with ​gold**' (*Theogony* 135) — one word of ‌ornament, and the only one he ever gives ​her. Then, at 371–374: 'Hyperion lay in ‌love with Theía of the gold crown, ​and she bore him great Hēlios and bright ‌Selḗnē and Ēōs, who brings light to ​all mortals and to the deathless gods.' ​That is the entirety of her recorded mythology ​— a birth, a marriage, three children ​— and it is enough to found ​a cosmology: the upper air wed to the ‌high one, and **every light that crosses ​the sky as their offspring**. Later Greek poets ‌repeat the triad without ever adding a ​scene; the goddess's silence in the tradition ‌may itself be the myth — **the medium ​of light does not appear; it makes ‌appearing possible**.[^2]

### Pindar's Theia of Many Names ​(The Golden Hymn)

Pindar opens *Isthmian* 5 with ‌the most vivid address Theía ever received: ​'**Mother of the Sun, Theia of many ​names**' — and immediately explains the 'many names': ‌it is because of her that mortals ‌count gold as the most powerful of things, ‌for the radiance of her doings shows ​upon gold and its gleam. The ancient ​scholiasts add the practical detail: sailors at sea ‌see Theía in the sun's distant flash ​on the waves, reading the horizon by ​her. The logic is antique and precise — ‌the goddess of the shining ether is ​present wherever light becomes visible as *radiance*: ​on metal, on water, on the glint that ‌betrays a ship over the horizon. Her ​epithet also hints at a theological elasticity: the ‌same luminous principle answers to whatever the ​moment requires — sight, splendor, the flash ​of gold. **Theía is not a character but ​an optics**, and Pindar hymns her as ​such.

### Sight, Wonder, and the Divine (Name ‌and Vision)

Ancient and modern scholars alike connect ‌Theía's name with **θέα, 'sight'**, and the ​verb θεάομαι, 'to gaze in wonder' — ‌the same root family as θέατρον, 'theater', and ​θεωρία, 'contemplation'. Later Greek writers could not ​resist the further step: that θεά, 'goddess', belongs ‌to the same family — the divine ‌as *that which shines forth and is ‌seen*. The second derivation is linguistically shaky, and ‌a scholarly entry must say so plainly; ​but the intuition was deeply Greek, and ‌Plato's vocabulary of the knowable as 'visible in ​its radiance' lives in the same semantic ​field. Her gold crown completes the picture: ​**the goddess of sight wears the substance that ‌most resembles what sight loves**. If her ​cult was negligible, her word-family conquered the language ​— theory, theater, and theology are all, ​etymologically, her daughters too.

### Among the Fallen ‌Titans (The Fall)

Hesiod does not show Theía ​fighting in the Titanomachy, but the arithmetic ​of *Theogony* 717–720 leaves her no exemption: ​after the ten-year war, Zeus's side bound the ‌Titans and hurled them 'into murky Tartarus, ​as far beneath the earth as earth ‌is beneath heaven'. The Titanesses as a group ​disappear from the poem into that fall ‌— while their luminous children ride on overhead, ​untouchable. Theía's fate, if she shared it, ‌is the cosmic version of her own ‌nature: **the ether cannot be imprisoned, but the ​personification can**. Later tradition quietly released her: ​she survives in Pindar and in the ​scholia as the ever-present mother of light, unshrined ​by any city but unexcluded from any ‌sky — a goddess whose temple is ‌whatever the light touches, and whose only liturgy ​is the daybreak itself.

sources.citation: Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek.
Hesiod, Theogony 135, 371–374.

syncretism.body:
Rome ​produced no ‌Theía ‌— Latin ​mythographers ​list her ​among ​the Titans ​(Hyginus, ‌*Fabulae* praefatio), ​but ​no Roman ‌cult ​developed and ‌no ​Roman equivalent ‌was ​invented; her ​name ​crossed into ​Latin ​only as ‌a learned ​genealogy. ‌In later ​antique ‌thought her ​province ‌was absorbed ​by ‌the radiance-cults ​around ​Sol and ‌by ‌Neoplatonic meditations ‌on ​light as ​the ‌first emanation. ​Her ​most striking ‌reception ​is modern: ​planetary ‌scientists named ​the ‌Mars-sized protoplanet ​of ​the **giant-impact ​hypothesis** ​— the ‌body ‌whose collision ​with ‌the infant ​Earth ​threw up ‌the ‌debris that ‌became ‌the Moon ​— ‌'**Theia**'. It ​is ​a strangely ​perfect ‌tribute: the ​Titaness of ​shining, ​invoked at ‌the ​birth of ​the ​very moon ‌her ​mythology first ‌explained.[^1]

​Within the ‌Greek ​tradition, closely ‌related ‌names in ​the ​corpus include ​[[acheron|Achérōn]], ​[[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], ‌[[adonis|Ádōnis]], ‌[[aer|Aḗr]], and ​[[aigyptos|Aígyptos]].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

cultural-legacy.body: Theía's ​afterlife ‌is linguistic ‌and ​scientific ​rather ​than ​cultic. From ​her ‌root-family ​come ​*theory*, *theater*, ‌and ​*theorem* ‌— ​the Greek ‌conviction ​that ​to ​see ​is to ​know, ‌and ​that ‌the highest ​knowing ‌is ​a ‌kind ​of beholding. ‌Her ​children ​gave ‌her a ‌permanent ‌gallery: ​every ​classical depiction ‌of ​Hēlios ​rising, ‌Selḗnē ​veiled, or ​Ēōs ‌in ​her ‌saffron robe ​is, ​indirectly, ​her ​portrait. ‌In the ‌twenty-first ​century ‌her ​name passed ​permanently ‌into ‌the ‌scientific lexicon ‌through ​the ‌Theia ​impact ​hypothesis — ​one ‌of ​the ​few Titanesses ​whose ‌name ​now ​appears ​in planetary-science ‌textbooks. ​Restoring ‌*Theía* ​restores the ‌name ​of ‌the ‌brightness that ​makes ​brightness ​possible: ​the ‌light before ‌the ​lamp.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

archaeology.body: No ​sanctuary ‌of ‌Theía ​is ​securely ​attested — ​Pausanias, ​who ‌tours ​hundreds ​of ‌shrines ​across ‌Greece, ​offers ‌her ​not one ​— ​and ​no ​independent ‌image ​of ‌her ​survives. ‌She ​is ‌visible only ​indirectly: ‌in ​the ​countless ‌representations ‌of ‌her ​children, ​Hēlios ‌rising ​in his ​chariot, ‌Selḗnē ​with ​billowing ‌veil, ​Ēōs ‌ascending ​in ​saffron, ​whose ​very ubiquity ‌is ‌her ​monument. ‌Her ​name ​is ‌fixed ‌for ‌us ‌instead ​by the ‌earliest ​Greek ​poetry ​— ‌the ​two ​lines ​of ‌Hesiod ​and ​the opening ​of ‌Pindar's ​fifth ‌Isthmian ​— ‌a ​reminder ‌that ‌some ​gods ​are monuments ​of ​language ‌rather ‌than ​stone.[^1]

meditation.body:
Theía ​is the ‌unseen ‌source of ​all ​that is ​seen. ​She has ​no ‌myths because ​her ​power is ‌too ​basic for ‌narrative: ​it is ‌the ​condition under ​which ​any story ​can ​be witnessed. ‌To ​honor ‌her is ​to ‌recognize that ​light ‌is not ​merely ‌physical but ​epistemic ​— we ‌know ‌by seeing, ‌and ​we are ​known ‌by being ​seen.

​Her restoration ‌in ​Unicode is ​fitting. ‌The very ​act ‌of reading ​a ​restored Greek ​name ​on a ‌screen ‌depends on ​light, ‌on sight, ​on ​luminous technology ‌that ‌her children ‌prefigured. ‌Theía reminds ​us ‌that behind ​every ​visible marvel ​there ‌is ​an older, ​quieter ​power: the ‌brightness ​that makes ​brightness ​possible. The ‌Greeks ​rarely prayed ‌to ​her; they ‌simply ​saw everything ‌by ‌her — ​which ​may be ​the ​purest form ‌of ‌worship there ​is.[^1]
